A scheme is <TEXTITOPEN_0001>quasi-compact<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if its underlying topological space is
quasi-compact. There is a relative notion which is defined as follows.

A morphism of schemes is called <TEXTITOPEN_0001>quasi-compact<TEXTITCLOSE_0001>
if the underlying map of topological spaces is
quasi-compact, see
Topology, Definition <REF_0001>.

Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of schemes.
The following are equivalent

<STRUCT_0004> there exists some affine open covering <MATH_0003>
such that <MATH_0004> is quasi-compact for all <MATH_0005>.

By compactness we can find finitely many points <MATH_0009>

union of affine opens. Since <MATH_0013> is a standard

Hence <MATH_0016> is affine, and so

<STRUCT_0001><STRUCT_0002>
Next, assume that the inverse image of every affine open is a finite
union of affine opens.
Let <MATH_0018> be any quasi-compact open. Since <MATH_0019> has a basis
of the topology consisting of affine opens we see that <MATH_0020> is a finite
union of affine opens. Hence the inverse image of <MATH_0021> is a finite
union of affine opens. Hence <MATH_0022> is quasi-compact.
